segments.text: Every time a helicopter's rotor turns, one of its blades is doing something that sounds impossible.
When the aircraft moves forward, the blade swinging toward the nose is carried along by
the aircraft and meets the air at the rotor's own speed, plus the helicopter's speed,
close to the speed of sound at the tip. The blade swinging back toward the tail meets the air at
the rotor's speed minus the helicopter's speed, which is almost nothing at the root.
The same machine asks one wing to fly fast and the other to barely fly, and it asks them to swap
every fraction of a second. So here is the question, why would anyone build an aircraft that needs this
much cleverness just to stay in the air, when a plane is simpler, faster, and cheaper? The answer
is that a helicopter is the only aircraft that can do three things at once, take off from a place no
bigger than itself, hover over a spot, and stop in the air. Everything else about it is the price of
those three abilities. Start with the lift, since that is the odd part. A plane's wings are fixed and
the air flows past them because the plane is moving. A helicopter has no forward motion in a hover,
so the wings themselves are made to move, and they turn in a circle above the cabin.
The blades are long, thin wings spun by an engine through a gearbox. They push air downward,
and the reaction holds the aircraft up. It is a simple idea, and it has a heavy bill,
because lifting a weight with a spinning wing takes a lot of power for every kilogram,
far more than a plane needs.
The second problem is built into the first. If a motor spins a rotor one way, the body of the
helicopter wants to spin the other way. That is why most helicopters have a small rotor on the tail,
which pushes sideways to stop the cabin from turning. It is a necessary nuisance. The tail rotor
takes power that could have gone to lifting. It is thin and exposed, and a hit to it can spin the
aircraft out of control. Designers have found other answers, such as two main rotors turning in opposite
directions, so the twisting forces cancel, and every answer changes what the helicopter can do.
The tandem version, with one rotor at the front and one at the back, is one such answer. It has a long
cabin, can carry heavy loads, and keeps its balance well when something heavy is hung on a hook.
A coaxial version stacks two rotors on top of one another, which gives a very compact machine that
has no tail rotor and can climb sharply. Each is a different bargain. The ordinary single rotor with a
tail is the cheapest and the most common, and so it ends up in most of the world's fleets.
Then there is the problem from the opening, which is the one that limits how fast a helicopter can go.
As the aircraft speeds up, the blade moving forward gets close to the speed of sound,
where the airflow becomes violent and drag rises sharply, while the blade moving backward loses
lift and begins to stall. Past a certain speed, the whole thing becomes unbalanced. That is why
conventional helicopters top out at speeds a regional airliner would think slow. It is not engine
power that stops them, it is the blades. To control all this, the pilot has three controls, and each
one is a small miracle of mechanics. One lever changes the angle of all the blades at once, which makes the
aircraft climb or sink. A stick tilts the whole rotor disc, which moves the helicopter forward, back or
sideways. Pedals change the tail rotor, which turns the nose. A blade must change its angle as it goes
around, increasing its bite when it is on one side, and reducing it on the other, and a plate under the
rotor head does this with every revolution. The rotor head, the part most people see as a simple hub,
is one of the busiest mechanisms on the aircraft. That complexity is why helicopters are so hungry for
maintenance. Almost everything that holds the aircraft up is a moving part under heavy load.
The blades, the head, the gearbox, the bearings, each has a limited number of hours before it must be
replaced, and each is checked often. A large share of the cost of owning a helicopter goes toward keeping
those parts within their limits, and a helicopter that is flying is usually one that has been worked
on a good deal more than it has flown. There is a safety trick hiding in all this, and it is why a
helicopter is less fragile than it looks. If the engine fails, the pilot drops the lever, and the air
rushing upward through the rotor keeps the blades turning by themselves, like a sycamore seed. The aircraft
descends fast, but under control, and at the last moment the pilot raises the lever and uses the stored
spin in the blades to cushion the landing. It is called autorotation, and every helicopter pilot
practices it until it is routine. Where a helicopter flies matters as much as how. The rotor needs dense
air to push against, and air is thinner when it is hot or high. On a summer afternoon in a mountain
valley, the same helicopter that lifted a full load at sea level may be unable to hover with half of it.
Crews in the mountains of Afghanistan learned this repeatedly, and planners there began to count not
only how heavy the load was, but what the temperature would be when it arrived. Dust is a second enemy.
A helicopter landing on dry ground throws up a cloud that can fill the cabin and hide the earth,
a condition called a brownout, and the same cloud is pulled into the engine, where fine sand wears the
blades and can ruin a turbine in a few hours. Filters and particle separators help, but they cost power.
A helicopter that works from deserts is a helicopter that spends a large part of its engine life being
cleaned. Fighting makes it worse, which is why military helicopters are built with an eye to being
hit. The crew sits in seats that absorb energy in a hard landing and are shielded by armor. Fuel
tanks are self-sealing, so a hole closes instead of leaking. The main gearbox, which sends engine power
to the rotor and would normally fail within minutes if its oil ran out, is designed to keep running for a
time without it. Some armed helicopters are required to be able to take rifle caliber hits in the rotor
and keep flying home. It is a machine that has accepted it will be shot at. The reason it will be
shot at is how it fights. A transport helicopter flies low, below the line of sight of radar,
using valleys, trees and buildings as cover. A practice called nap of the earth flying. A gunship can
hover behind a hill, pop up to fire a missile and drop back down. In that sense, the helicopter is the
opposite of the fighter. It does not win by speed and height. It wins by being in a place where no
one expected an aircraft and by leaving before they have time to react. That tactic has a modern flaw.
The same trees and hills that hide a helicopter also hide the people who shoot it. A man with a
shoulder-launched missile, standing in a field, can bring down a machine worth tens of millions of
dollars. Radar does not see low, but a person with a tube and a pair of ears does. Against modern air
defenses, low flying has become more dangerous, and some armies have started to question whether
a gunship can survive near an enemy that has such weapons. The answer depends on the other side's
imagination more than its budget. There is also a hybrid that tries to avoid the whole problem.
The tilt rotor has large rotors on the wingtips that point up for takeoff, like a helicopter,
and then tilt forward to work as propellers, so the aircraft flies like a plane. It is faster and goes much
farther than a helicopter. It is also more complex, heavier to maintain and costlier, and its rotors
are so large that they blow dust and debris about, in a way that has caused trouble. The bargain here
is clear, it gives up simplicity to get speed and range. Which brings us to what is easy to get wrong.
People assume a helicopter is a slow, clumsy plane. A better way to see it is as a vehicle, closer to a
truck than to a fighter, that happens to fly. Its job is not to cross the sky, but to arrive at one
specific piece of ground, wherever that happens to be, and to do so without a runway. That is my own
reading, but it suggests that the question to ask of a helicopter is not how fast it flies, but how
little it needs from the ground. So return to the blade that has to fly fast on one side and almost
not at all on the other. Every part, the tail rotor, the plate under the head, the armored seat and the
gearbox that runs dry, is there to keep a machine going that asks the air for too much. A helicopter is
not a gift of physics. It is an argument with it that the engineers keep winning, one flight at a time.
